Source: SkyNRG (2025) 2.2 Sustainable/Synthetic Aviation Fuel Market Analysis There are multiple market factors that influence fuel adoption, including price (relative to conventional fuel), availability, compatibility, emissions, and policy factors. SAF is the sole alternative fuel currently used commercially, and key barriers to adoption include availability and price. SAF prices are currently stated as 2 to 5 times higher than conventional jet fuel prices 32 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. snollaG noilliM 2,000 1,800 1,600 1,400 1,200 1,000 800 600 400 200 0 United States European Union United Kingdom Asia Latin America snollaG noilliM (World Economic Forum 2024); therefore, policy has been a key factor in enabling SAF (Section 2.2.2). The low availability of SAF reflects the higher costs of production, competition for feedstock with renewable diesel and other products, and long lead times to develop and build biorefineries. The availability of capital and federal loan guarantees to build and demonstrate first-of-a-kind aviation “fuel” plants will impact markets and the timeliness of deploying new fuels to the aviation market. 2.2.1 SAF Production, Consumption, and Commercial Plants SAF has been commercially available since 2016, with substantial new production capacity coming online in late 2024 and early 2025 (Table 4 and Table 5). Nearly all existing SAF plants utilize the HEFA pathway for production. As of 2025, there are six domestic commercial plants and one international producer, Neste, supplying the U.S. market. Three of the plants are conversions of petroleum refineries—World Energy, Montana Renewables, and Phillips 66— while Diamond Green Diesel, LanzaJet, and New Rise Renewables are new plants. Neste has exported to the U.S. market since 2020 (Neste 2020). ICAO provides a list of global SAF plants in development stages, self-reported with specific requirements (ICAO 2025b).5 The international plants are owned and operated by various petroleum companies and were either conversions of existing refineries or modifications to enable coprocessing SAF alongside petroleum products (Table 5).
